blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A function call is a function’s name followed by round brackets. The values written inside the brackets are its arguments, and the call returns one result, which R prints or which you assign to a name.

Each argument has a name. An argument may be given by name, as digits = 1, or by position, in the order the function lists its arguments.

Most arguments have a default value, which is used when the call does not give one. For mean(), median() and sd(), the argument na.rm says whether missing values (NA) are removed before the computation. Its default, FALSE, makes the result NA whenever a value is missing.

A help page, opened with ?name or help(name), describes one function in fixed sections: Description, Usage, Arguments, Value (what it returns) and Examples.

blocks.label: In plain terms
blocks.html:
heights_cm <- c(152, 160.5, 171)
mean(heights_cm)
[1] 161.1667

Whatever goes inside the brackets is an argument. Many functions take more than one. round() takes the number to round, called x, and how many decimal places to keep, called digits:

round(161.1667, digits = 1)
[1] 161.2

Leave out an argument altogether and R uses its default. The default for digits is 0, so round(161.1667) gives a whole number.

One call can sit inside another, and R works from the inside out:

round(mean(heights_cm), digits = 1)
[1] 161.2

The pipe, written |>, puts the steps in the order they happen. Read it as “then”. Type it as two characters, | then >. A line that ends in |> is unfinished, so R waits for the next line, as with the + prompt in section 2. The indent is only for reading:

heights_cm |>
  mean() |>
  round(digits = 1)
[1] 161.2

The pipe hands the thing on its left to the call on its right, as the first argument. So round(digits = 1) here means round(the mean, digits = 1).

To find out what a function’s arguments are called and what they do, open its help page. Type a question mark and the name: ?round.

blocks.alt: A bar chart with three bars: missing weight typed as 0, mean, 3392.5 g; na.rm = TRUE, mean, 3769.444 g; na.rm = TRUE, median, 3650 g.
blocks.caption: The same ten body masses, with penguin 4 missing, summarised three ways. Typing the missing weight as 0 gives a mean of 3392.5 g. Leaving it out with na.rm = TRUE gives a mean of 3769.444 g and a median of 3650 g, both from 9 values.

blocks.label: Illustration 1
blocks.html:
Start where the last section stopped. Here again are the first ten body masses in the practice file, in grams, with the fourth missing. Ask for their mean:

body_mass_g <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250)
mean(body_mass_g)
[1] NA

NA again. Open the help page:

?mean

Read the Usage section first. It shows the call with every argument and its default: mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE, ...). Then read Arguments, which says what each one does. na.rm is “a logical evaluating to ‘TRUE’ or ‘FALSE’ indicating whether ‘NA’ values should be stripped before the computation proceeds”. Its default is FALSE: do not remove them. That is why one missing value made the mean NA. You did not ask for anything to be removed.

Ask for it:

mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 3769.444

Now look at what that number is. It is not the mean of ten values. Check it with the tools from the last section, adding the known values and dividing by how many there are:

known_g <- body_mass_g[!is.na(body_mass_g)]
sum(known_g)
length(known_g)
sum(known_g) / length(known_g)
[1] 33925
[1] 9
[1] 3769.444

The nine known masses add up to 33925 g, and 33925 divided by 9 is the same 3769.444 g. So na.rm = TRUE changed the count behind the mean from ten to nine. That is the honest answer, as long as you report the nine with it. A short way to count the values that are present is to add up a logical vector. In arithmetic R counts each TRUE as 1 and each FALSE as 0:

sum(!is.na(body_mass_g))
[1] 9

Here is the dishonest answer, which is easy to reach by accident. Suppose whoever typed the register wrote 0 where the weight was not taken:

body_mass_zero_g <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, 0, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250)
mean(body_mass_zero_g)
[1] 3392.5

No warning, no NA, and a number that looks like a body mass. It is the 33925 g divided by 10, not by 9, as though one penguin weighed nothing. And median() has the same argument:

median(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 3650
how the missing value was handled result (g)
missing weight typed as 0, mean 3392.5
na.rm = TRUE, mean 3769.444
na.rm = TRUE, median 3650

Last, put the steps together for a report in kilograms. Nested, it reads inside out. Piped, it reads in order: take the masses, then convert to kilograms, then take the mean of the known values, then round to two decimal places.

round(mean(body_mass_g / 1000, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 2)

(body_mass_g / 1000) |>
  mean(na.rm = TRUE) |>
  round(digits = 2)
[1] 3.77
[1] 3.77

Both give 3.77 kg. The sentence for the report is “mean body mass 3.77 kg (n = 9)”.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html:
The ten masses are real rows of the practice file. The register with a 0 typed in is made up, to show what a zero does to a mean.

na.rm = TRUE gives the mean of the values present. It is the mean of all ten only if the missing one would have sat at that same mean, and nothing here can tell you whether it would. Which values go missing, and why, is a question for a later book in this course.

blocks.label: Illustration 2
blocks.html:
Error messages are about a call. Read them as sentences. Leave out an argument that has no default:

mean()
Error in mean.default() : argument "x" is missing, with no default

The message names the function (mean.default is the version of mean() that handles plain numbers) and says exactly what is wrong: the argument x is missing and has no default.

Misspell a value:

mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = true)
Error: object 'true' not found

R knows TRUE in capitals. To it, true is the name of an object, and no object with that name exists. Give a function the wrong kind of value:

round("3.77", digits = 1)
Error in round("3.77", digits = 1) :
  non-numeric argument to mathematical function

round() needs a number and was given text.

Errors are the friendly failures, because they stop you. The dangerous mistake is the call that runs. Suppose you want the mean of three body masses and forget c():

mean(3750, 3800, 3250)
[1] 3750

No error and no warning, and 3750 g is a believable body mass. It is wrong. Without c(), the three numbers are three separate arguments, matched by position. mean() took 3750 as x, 3800 as its second argument, trim, and 3250 went into the ... that collects extra arguments. The help page says trim is “the fraction (0 to 0.5) of observations to be trimmed from each end of ‘x’ before the mean is computed”, and that values outside that range are taken as the nearest end. So trim became 0.5, and the “mean” of the single value 3750 is 3750. The call you meant:

mean(c(3750, 3800, 3250))
[1] 3600

The mean of the three is 3600 g.

blocks.label: Where this picture breaks
blocks.html: Not every wrong call is silent and not every one errors; which happens depends on the function. The trim behaviour is particular to mean(). The general lesson is to put the values you mean to combine inside c() and to name every argument after the first.

points.html: The error is to read mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) as the mean of all your values. It is the mean of the values present. Report the count with it, “3.77 kg (n = 9)”, every time.
A missing value typed as 0 gives no NA and no warning, and pulls the mean down.

Name every argument after the first. round(x, digits = 1) says what the 1 is. mean(3750, 3800, 3250) runs, gives 3750 and is wrong, because unnamed values were matched by position to arguments you did not intend.
Before you use a function for the first time, open its help page and read Usage and Arguments.
Read an error message as a sentence about one call: which function, which argument, what was wrong. Fix that argument and nothing else, then run the line again.
No argument can tell you why a value is missing.
If you find yourself copying the same block of calls three times with one thing changed, you need a function of your own. Writing one is taught in a later book in this course.

blocks.prompt: A first-year resident has ten minutes and R open. They have never read a help page. Teach them to find out, from ?round alone, what round(3.14159) will give and why.
blocks.answer:
Ask them to type ?round and look at the page with you. Point to three parts in turn.

Description says, in one line, that round rounds “to the specified number of decimal places (default 0)”.

Usage shows the call written out with its defaults: round(x, digits = 0). Ask them what digits = 0 means. It means that if they give no digits, R uses 0.

Arguments says what x and digits are. Ask them to predict round(3.14159) from that. No digits is given, so the default 0 applies, and the answer is a whole number, 3. Then let them run it:

round(3.14159)
round(3.14159, digits = 2)
[1] 3
[1] 3.14

Finish by asking them to run one line from the Examples section at the bottom of the page. The habit to leave them with: Usage for the defaults, Arguments for what each one does, Examples to try it.

blocks.prompt: Without looking back, say what na.rm = TRUE does in mean(x, na.rm = TRUE) and what its default is. Then say what you must report beside a mean computed this way.
blocks.answer: It removes the missing values before the mean is computed. The default is na.rm = FALSE, which gives NA whenever a value is missing. Because the mean is then of the values present, report how many there were, as in “3.77 kg (n = 9)”.

blocks.prompt: A made-up adult’s BMI is 24.83702 kg/m2. Write one call that rounds it to one decimal place and one that rounds it to a whole number.
blocks.answer:
round(24.83702, digits = 1)
round(24.83702)
[1] 24.8
[1] 25

With no digits, round() uses its default, 0, and gives a whole number.

blocks.prompt: Find the mean of the four numbers 4, 8, a missing value and 6, with the default behaviour. Then find it using only the values that are present.
blocks.answer:
mean(c(4, 8, NA, 6))
mean(c(4, 8, NA, 6), na.rm = TRUE)
[1] NA
[1] 6

The default gives NA. With na.rm = TRUE, R averages 4, 8 and 6, which sum to 18, and 18 divided by 3 is 6.

blocks.prompt:
Rewrite this nested call with the pipe, one step per line, and check that it gives the same answer.

round(mean(c(61.2, 58.4, 70.9)), digits = 1)
blocks.answer:
round(mean(c(61.2, 58.4, 70.9)), digits = 1)

c(61.2, 58.4, 70.9) |>
  mean() |>
  round(digits = 1)
[1] 63.5
[1] 63.5

The innermost call, mean(), comes first in the pipe. Each pipe hands the result on as the first argument of the next call.

blocks.prompt: The first ten flipper lengths in penguins_raw.csv are 181, 186, 195, a missing value, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193 and 190 mm. Give their mean and their median in centimetres, each to one decimal place, and say how many values each is based on.
blocks.answer:
flipper_mm <- c(181, 186, 195, NA, 193, 190, 181, 195, 193, 190)
flipper_cm <- flipper_mm / 10
round(mean(flipper_cm, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 1)
round(median(flipper_cm, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 1)
sum(!is.na(flipper_cm))
[1] 18.9
[1] 19
[1] 9

The mean is 18.9 cm and the median is 19 cm, each from the 9 rows whose flipper length is recorded. R prints 19 rather than 19.0: a single value is printed without a trailing zero.

blocks.prompt: Using only the help page of sd(), find how to make it leave out missing values. The first ten body masses in penguins_raw.csv are 3750, 3800, 3250, a missing value, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475 and 4250 g. Give their standard deviation, rounded to the nearest gram.
blocks.answer:
The Usage section of ?sd reads sd(x, na.rm = FALSE), and Arguments says na.rm decides whether missing values are removed. The default is FALSE, so set it to TRUE:

body_mass_g <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250)
round(sd(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE))
[1] 440

The standard deviation of the 9 known body masses is 440 g. In Book 0, a standard deviation from a sample divides by one less than the count. The help page says sd() does the same: “Like ‘var’ this uses denominator n - 1.”

blocks.prompt: Without using mean(), write code that gives the same number as mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE) for the ten body masses in problem 5. Then show that the two agree.
blocks.answer:
body_mass_g <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250)
known_g <- body_mass_g[!is.na(body_mass_g)]
sum(known_g) / length(known_g)
mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 3769.444
[1] 3769.444

Both give 3769.444 g. Removing the missing value first and then dividing by the count of what is left is exactly what na.rm = TRUE does.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague wants the mean of three body masses. Their code and output are below, and they report “the mean body mass was 3750 g”. Find what broke, and say why the answer looks reasonable.

mean(3750, 3800, 3250)
[1] 3750
blocks.answer:
The three numbers are not inside c(), so they are three separate arguments. R matched them by position: 3750 became x, 3800 became trim, and 3250 went into .... A trim above 0.5 is taken as 0.5. x is the single value 3750, and any mean of one value, trimmed or not, is that value.

mean(c(3750, 3800, 3250))
[1] 3600

The mean is 3600 g. The wrong answer looks reasonable because 3750 g is one of the masses. It lies inside the range of the data, and R gave no warning.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague’s script stops at this line. The error is below. Find what broke.

body_mass_g <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450)
mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = true)
Error: object 'true' not found
blocks.answer:
R’s logical values are written in capitals, TRUE and FALSE. Written in small letters, true is read as the name of an object, and there is no object called true.

mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 3562.5

The mean of the four known masses is 3562.5 g. The error message gave the answer: it names the word R could not find.

blocks.prompt:
A colleague reports the mean of the first ten body masses (problem 5) in kilograms, to two decimal places, as 3.78 kg. Their code and output are below. Find what broke, and say why the answer looks reasonable.

body_mass_g <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250)
round(body_mass_g / 1000) |>
  mean(na.rm = TRUE) |>
  round(digits = 2)
[1] 3.78
blocks.answer:
The masses were rounded to whole kilograms before the mean was taken. Each value lost up to half a kilogram first, and only then were the values averaged. Look at what went into the mean:

round(body_mass_g / 1000)
 [1]  4  4  3 NA  3  4  4  5  3  4

Round once, at the end:

(body_mass_g / 1000) |>
  mean(na.rm = TRUE) |>
  round(digits = 2)
[1] 3.77

The mean of the 9 known masses is 3.77 kg. The wrong answer looks reasonable because it has the digits asked for and is only 0.01 kg away. It came from whole numbers, though, so its second decimal place means nothing. This is Book 0’s rule again: keep full precision while you work and round once, at the end.

blocks.prompt: A made-up draft report says: “The average body mass in the first ten rows was 3392.5 g.” The first ten body masses are as in problem 5. Work out with code how that number could have been produced. Say what the sentence gets wrong, and what a corrected sentence still does not establish.
blocks.answer:
3392.5 is lower than every one of the nine known masses except 3250 g, which is a sign that something pulled it down. Try dividing the total of the known masses by ten instead of nine:

body_mass_g <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250)
known_g <- body_mass_g[!is.na(body_mass_g)]
sum(known_g) / 10
mean(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
[1] 3392.5
[1] 3769.444

The report’s number is the total of nine masses divided by ten: the missing weight was treated as zero. A corrected sentence: “The mean body mass of the 9 rows with a recorded weight was 3769.4 g.”

What the corrected sentence does not establish:

  • The mean of all ten. Penguin 4’s weight is unknown, and it could lie anywhere.
  • Anything about the penguins in the rest of the file, or about penguins in general.

blocks.prompt: A made-up thesis table reports “median body mass 3650 g (n = 10)” for the first ten rows of the practice file. The values are as in problem 5. Check both numbers with code, and say what the checked result does not establish.
blocks.answer:
body_mass_g <- c(3750, 3800, 3250, NA, 3450, 3650, 3625, 4675, 3475, 4250)
median(body_mass_g, na.rm = TRUE)
sum(!is.na(body_mass_g))
[1] 3650
[1] 9

The median, 3650 g, is right. The n is wrong: the median was computed from 9 values, not 10, because na.rm = TRUE removed the missing one. The table should read “3650 g (n = 9)”. The writer probably took n from length(body_mass_g), which counts the missing value too.

What the checked result does not establish:

  • The median of all ten values. With a tenth value, the median would be the mean of the two middle values, and that depends on the missing weight.
  • Anything about penguins beyond these ten rows.
